description: Severity distribution for slips, trips, and stumbles WITHOUT fall to lower level. Person stays on the same level — falls to ground from standing height. The highest-frequency workplace event but mostly non-SIF. P(death) scale from AIS mortality data.
assumptions: Same-level fall from standing height (~1.5-1.8m head height)
No secondary hazard (no adjacent edge, machinery, traffic, water)
magnitude_note: Same-level falls have roughly constant gravitational energy (standing height). Severity variation comes from landing surface, secondary hazards, and body orientation on impact. Bands defined by context rather than energy magnitude.

magnitude_bands.description: Indoor same-level slip/trip on flat surface. Office, warehouse, corridor, shop floor. Typical wet floor, cable trip, uneven mat.
magnitude_bands.mortality_source: HSE RIDDOR data; BLS nonfatal injury survey. Same-level falls are #1 cause of workplace injury by frequency but <1% result in serious injury. Fatalities almost exclusively elderly or secondary mechanism (hit head on furniture).
magnitude_bands.rationale: Most indoor slips produce bruising or minor sprains. P50=first_aid (ice pack, minor sprain). P90=medical_treatment reflects wrist/ankle fracture from bracing. Head strike onto hard floor is the SIF pathway but rare enough to not reach P90 for a working-age adult.

magnitude_bands.description: Outdoor same-level slip/trip on uneven or hazardous surface. Construction site, kerb, gravel, ice, mud, slopes, decking. Higher energy transfer from uneven ground and inability to brace.
magnitude_bands.mortality_source: HSE construction injury data; winter slip-and-fall studies. Outdoor falls on hard/uneven surfaces produce more fractures than indoor, but fatality remains rare for working-age.
magnitude_bands.rationale: Similar to indoor but higher fracture rate from uneven ground (can't control the fall). P90 at 0.01 reflects hip/wrist fracture on concrete or ice. Still well below SIF threshold for working-age adults.

magnitude_bands.description: Same-level slip/trip adjacent to a secondary hazard. Near platform edge, open water, machinery, traffic, excavation, chemical spill. The slip itself is low energy but the secondary exposure creates SIF potential.
magnitude_bands.mortality_source: OSHA/HSE fatality investigations where root cause was a slip/trip but fatality mechanism was the secondary hazard (fell into water, into machinery, off edge, into traffic).
magnitude_bands.rationale: The slip is non-SIF but proximity to a secondary hazard creates SIF potential. P90=serious_injury reflects the 10% of such events where the slip leads to secondary exposure (into water, over edge, into machinery). Note: if the secondary event occurs, it should be reclassified to that mechanism (fall, caught_in, etc.). This band captures the potential.

age.description: Multiplier on P(death). Same-level falls are a leading cause of death in over-65s due to osteoporosis (hip fracture mortality ~20-30% at 1 year) and anticoagulant use (intracranial bleeding from minor head strike). For workplace context, this modifier applies to elderly workers or public-facing environments.

surface.description: Multiplier on P(death). Harder surfaces produce more severe impact injuries. Ice adds uncontrolled fall dynamics.

carrying_load.description: Multiplier on P(death). Carrying a load prevents bracing during fall, increasing head-strike risk.

sources.author: HSE
sources.relevance: Slips and trips statistics — highest frequency workplace injury category in UK. RIDDOR data on same-level fall outcomes.

sources.author: BLS
sources.relevance: Survey of Occupational Injuries and Illnesses — same-level falls are #1 nonfatal injury event in US.

sources.author: OSHA
sources.relevance: ITA Case Detail: 88,678 same-level fall events in 2024 data. Event code 43.

sources.author: Baker et al.
sources.relevance: AIS mortality rates — foundation for P(death) scale

validation_notes: STKY check: same-level slip on wet floor should be NON_SIF — indoor_level P(SIF)=0.001 ✓
STKY check: slip near open excavation edge should be ELEVATED — near_secondary_hazard P(SIF)=0.10 ✓
Cross-check: OSHA ITA 2024 has 88,678 same-level falls with 0 fatalities out of ~689K total events — consistent with <0.001 fatality rate

The secondary hazard band is important: many 'slip' fatalities in investigation reports are really fall/caught_in/drowning events with a slip as the initiating mechanism. The classifier should ideally identify the dominant energy, not the initiating event.
